planting.note: Plant small container stock in fall on a lean, rocky, sharply drained slope; this species is notoriously intolerant of summer irrigation and overly rich soil, so resist amending the planting hole.

directions: Roundleaf buffaloberry is endemic to the Colorado Plateau and Great Basin pinyon-juniper woodlands, where it grows on raw gypsum, shale, and limestone outcrops among Pinus monophylla and Juniperus osteosperma. Its rounded, silver-felted leaves and naturally compact, mounding form give it strong year-round ornamental value in rock gardens and xeric borders without any pruning. It is extremely sensitive to root disturbance and summer water, so container-grown plants should be set out while small and left strictly alone once established. Small yellow flowers in early spring are followed by inconspicuous red berries on female plants where a male is nearby.

planting.note: Fall-sow onto lean, rocky, well-drained soil so seed overwinters and stratifies naturally; this species needs cold-moist stratification to break dormancy.

directions: Powder blue beardtongue grows on limestone and shale outcrops in pinyon-juniper and sagebrush communities across the Great Basin, forming a tidy evergreen rosette of thick, glaucous, powder-blue leaves that is attractive even without bloom. In late spring it sends up short spikes of deep violet-blue tubular flowers that are a strong hummingbird and native bee draw. It demands sharp drainage and resents both winter wet and summer irrigation, making it a reliable choice for rock gardens, crevice plantings, and dry gravel beds in cold, arid climates. Shear off spent flower stalks after bloom to keep the foliage rosette tidy.

planting.note: Fall-sow onto rocky, gravelly, sharply drained soil and leave uncovered; the seed needs winter cold-moist stratification and light to germinate.

directions: Granite prickly phlox is a low, woody-based subshrub common in the understory of pinyon-juniper woodland and on rocky slopes across the Great Basin, recognized by its stiff, needle-like leaf clusters and fragrant, phlox-like white-to-pale-lavender flowers that open in the evening. It thrives in pure gravel or decomposed granite with essentially no supplemental water once roots are established, making it well suited to dry rock gardens and slope plantings in cold-winter climates. The sharp foliage deters browsing, so it is a durable choice where deer or rabbit pressure is heavy. Avoid rich soil or mulch against the crown, both of which promote rot.

planting.note: Fall-sow onto lean, rocky or sandy soil for natural winter stratification; established plants need no irrigation beyond natural precipitation.

directions: Slender buckwheat is a wiry, mat-to-mound-forming subshrub found throughout pinyon-juniper and sagebrush communities of the Great Basin, with narrow gray-green leaves and clustered umbels of small cream to pink flowers from midsummer into fall. It is one of the most reliable late-season nectar sources for native bees and butterflies in a region where little else is blooming, and the dried flower heads age to attractive rust tones that persist into winter. It tolerates poor, rocky, and alkaline soils that defeat most garden perennials, asking only for full sun and sharp drainage. Cut back old flowering stems in late winter to keep the clump compact.

planting.note: Fall-sow or transplant small container stock onto dry, rocky-to-sandy soil in full sun; established plants resprout vigorously after fire or hard pruning.

directions: Yellow rabbitbrush is a small, rounded, resinous-leaved shrub common in openings and disturbed ground within pinyon-juniper and sagebrush woodlands across the Great Basin, distinguished from the larger rubber rabbitbrush by its slender twisted leaves and flatter flower clusters. Dense clusters of bright yellow flowers cover the shrub from late summer into fall, providing one of the last major nectar sources for migrating butterflies and native bees before frost. It is extremely drought- and cold-tolerant, resprouts readily after being cut back hard, and is useful for erosion control or filling in dry slopes where little else will establish. Avoid overwatering, which shortens its lifespan and makes it floppy.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or divided stock in fall; this rhizomatous shrub spreads slowly to form loose thickets and tolerates the dappled shade found under scattered pinyon and juniper canopy.

directions: Mountain snowberry occupies the cooler, slightly moister draws and north slopes within Great Basin pinyon-juniper woodland, often forming the shrub layer beneath scattered trees alongside Amelanchier and Cercocarpus. Small pink, bell-shaped flowers in early summer attract bees and hummingbirds, followed by white berries that persist into winter and feed birds after most other food sources are gone. It spreads gently by rhizome to form a loose, informal thicket useful for wildlife hedging or slope stabilization, and tolerates both the dry shade under conifers and open sun. Cut out old, woody stems every few years to keep new growth vigorous.

planting.note: Nick or scarify the hard seed coat and fall-sow onto lean, rocky soil; like most milkvetches it resents root disturbance, so start where it is to grow or in deep pots.

directions: Utah milkvetch forms a low, silvery-haired cushion of foliage on open, rocky ground within pinyon-juniper and sagebrush woodland across the eastern Great Basin, blooming in early spring with dense heads of magenta-pink pea flowers held just above the leaves. The compact habit and showy, early color make it a good candidate for dry rock gardens and crevice plantings in cold-winter climates, though like many milkvetches it is intolerant of summer irrigation and heavy soil. As a legume it fixes its own nitrogen and needs no fertilizer. Inflated, papery seed pods follow bloom and can be left in place to self-sow in gravelly ground.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall on a rocky, well-drained slope or canyon side; this is a slow-growing evergreen best sited where it can be left undisturbed long-term.

directions: Ashy silktassel grows on rocky slopes and canyon walls within pinyon-juniper woodland and chaparral of the eastern Sierra Nevada, Mojave, and Great Basin fringe, valued as one of the few broadleaf evergreen shrubs reliably hardy in this cold, dry woodland zone. Its leathery, gray-green leaves give year-round structure, and pendulous catkins of small greenish flowers appear in late winter on male and female plants, followed by blue-black berries on females. It is slow to establish and best planted small, after which it needs little beyond occasional deep watering through its first few dry summers. Use it as a background evergreen in a dry woodland or native shrub border where little else holds color through winter.
